events.title: The Edict of Nantes
events.shortBlurb: King Henry IV granted the French Protestants a measure of toleration, ending decades of religious war…
body: On 13 April 1598 King Henry IV of France signed the Edict of Nantes, closing nearly forty years of religious war that had begun with the massacre of Vassy in 1562. Henry, raised a Protestant and king of Navarre, had abjured that faith in 1593 to take the French crown; the edict was his settlement between the two religions of his realm.

In ninety-two public and fifty-six secret articles it granted the Huguenots freedom of conscience, public worship in places where it was already established, though not in Paris or at court, and equal access to offices, schools, and hospitals, while restoring Catholic worship where it had lapsed. By separate warrants the crown also granted them about a hundred fortified towns as places of surety, La Rochelle first among them.

The settlement pleased neither side — Pope Clement VIII said that it crucified him — but it gave France nearly ninety years of uneasy peace. Louis XIV revoked the edict in 1685 by the Edict of Fontainebleau, and as many as four hundred thousand Huguenots fled abroad, carrying their skills to England, Holland, and Prussia.
